passage: I'm Wasim, and last term maths felt like sand slipping through my fingers. Numbers wouldn't stay put. If Ammi said "Be back by quarter to six," I didn't know what that looked like on the clock. In class, when Arnab Sir said "Quick, how many minutes till lunch?", my chest went tight and my mind went white. But I could draw anything. My notebook margins were full of horses. Then Arnab Sir stopped asking me quick questions in front of everyone. He gave me a cardboard clock with hands I could move, and we counted in fives with bottle caps, again and again, no scolding. Now I can find quarter to six. I drew a horse on that cardboard clock, right at the six.

qa.q: What did Arnab Sir give Wasim to practise with?
qa.a: A cardboard clock with hands Wasim could move.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when asked a quick maths question in class, and what shows it?
qa.a: Panic; Wasim's chest went tight and Wasim's mind went white.

qa.q: Which change by Arnab Sir made progress possible?
qa.a: He stopped the quick public questions and used hands-on things like the clock and bottle caps, repeating patiently without scolding.

qa.q: How might Arnab Sir see Wasim's horse drawing on the clock?
qa.a: He may see it as a sign that Wasim now feels safe and even proud around the clock that once caused panic.

grounding: It shows a child who struggles with time and numbers and panics in maths though good at art, helped by hands-on materials, repetition and no shaming.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 4B, class shop week Rafiq priced the pencils beautifully; his labels had drawings of each item. But when Mehak bought an eraser for seven rupees with a ten-rupee coin, Rafiq froze. He counted the coins in the box three times, went red and whispered, "I can't do it." He left the counter and hid in the reading corner. In writing time the same afternoon he wrote a funny story about a shopkeeper parrot, full of lively words. What I did next: I gave Rafiq a tray of real coins and a number line, and we practised change privately, one small amount a day. No one is timed at the shop now. By Friday he gave three rupees change, checked it twice, and grinned. - Madhuri, class teacher

qa.q: How much did the eraser cost in the class shop?
qa.a: Seven rupees.

qa.q: What does Rafiq hiding in the reading corner suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt panic and embarrassment when he couldn't work out the change in front of others.

qa.q: What small steps did Madhuri take that helped Rafiq?
qa.a: Madhuri gave him real coins and a number line, practised privately one small amount a day, and stopped timing children at the shop.

qa.q: How might Mehak have been affected if Madhuri had scolded Rafiq at the counter?
qa.a: Mehak and the other children might have learned to see Rafiq as slow, and his shame would have grown.

grounding: A teacher sees a child who panics over money though he is strong in writing, and uses hands-on coins and patient repetition without shaming.

passage: In the kasba school near Rampur, the maths period began, and Hafsa's palms went damp. Avni Didi drew a clock and asked, "How many minutes till twelve?" The hands looked like they were sliding. Hafsa stared at her slate and said nothing, her ears burning. Yet that same morning she had written a poem about the monsoon that Avni Didi read aloud twice. After class, Avni Didi brought out a jar of tamarind seeds and a paper clock with a moving hand. "Tomorrow and every day, ten minutes, just us." She never said "careless." By the end of the month Hafsa could count out thirty seeds in fives and move the paper hand to half past.

qa.q: What did Avni Didi bring out after class?
qa.a: She brought out a jar of tamarind seeds and a paper clock with a moving hand.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when asked about the minutes till twelve?
qa.a: She felt panicked and embarrassed; her palms were damp, her ears burned and she could not answer.

qa.q: Why did Avni Didi's approach work?
qa.a: She used hands-on seeds and a paper clock, repeated it patiently every day and never called Hafsa careless, so Hafsa could make progress.

qa.q: How might Avni Didi see Hafsa, given the monsoon poem?
qa.a: Avni Didi sees a gifted writer who struggles with numbers, not a lazy or dull student.

grounding: Shows a child who panics over time and quantity despite a gift for language, making progress through hands-on materials and patient, shame-free repetition.

passage: In Cebu, Paulo, nine, missed the school bus again because he could not tell when "a quarter to" was. In the maths quiz the next morning, the numbers blurred and his chest went tight; he drew a robot in the margin instead. His cousin Sami, home from college, found the quiz in his bag. Paulo waited for the scolding. Instead Sami cut a clock from a paper plate and strung twenty beads on a shoelace. "We'll do this every night after dinner. Slowly." Paulo's comic about the robot was taped to the fridge by then, and Sami asked him to draw the bus arriving at a quarter to.

qa.q: Why did Paulo miss the school bus?
qa.a: He could not tell when "a quarter to" was.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling when Sami found the quiz?
qa.a: He felt scared and ashamed, waiting to be scolded for the blank maths quiz.

qa.q: What did Sami do that could help Paulo improve?
qa.a: Sami made a paper-plate clock and a bead string and planned slow practice every night, without scolding him.

qa.q: How does Sami seem to see Paulo's talents?
qa.a: Sami values Paulo's drawing and uses it, asking him to draw the bus arriving at a quarter to.

grounding: Shows a child who struggles with time and quantity and freezes in maths but is gifted at art, helped by hands-on tools and patient, unshaming practice.

passage: In the school's resource room, Ojas, eleven, wrote "21" when Asif Sir had said "twelve," then rubbed it out so hard the page tore. "I'm useless at this," he muttered. In English class he had just won the story prize, but numbers never stayed where he put them. Asif Sir did not sigh. He tipped a box of wooden blocks onto the table. "Build twelve for me. One ten-rod, two little cubes." Ojas built it. Then twenty-one. He looked at both side by side for a long time. "They're not the same at all," he said slowly. They built numbers again the next day, and the next.

qa.q: What did Ojas write when Asif Sir said "twelve"?
qa.a: He wrote "21" and then rubbed it out so hard the page tore.

qa.q: What does Ojas rubbing the page so hard suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and ashamed, calling himself useless even though he is good at writing stories.

qa.q: Which part of Asif Sir's response helped most?
qa.a: He did not sigh or shame Ojas; he used wooden blocks so Ojas could see and build the difference, and repeated it each day.

qa.q: How might Asif Sir see Ojas as a learner?
qa.a: Asif Sir likely sees a capable boy who needs to handle numbers with his hands, not someone who is useless.

grounding: Shows a child who struggles to grasp quantity despite strength in language, progressing with hands-on materials and patient repetition.

passage:
Monday. When Baljeet Sir wrote 47 minus 19 on the board, Tejas's stomach twisted. The numbers seemed to slide around. He stared out of the window and stopped listening, though his notebook margins were full of beautiful drawn birds.
Wednesday. Baljeet Sir kept him back, not to scold. He put a tray of matchsticks, tied in bundles of ten, on the desk. "Show me forty-seven." Tejas counted bundles slowly. Then he untied one to take nineteen away. "Twenty-eight," he whispered.
The next Monday. They did it again, and again, with the matchsticks and then with drawings of birds in groups of ten. When Tejas got a sum right on the board, nobody laughed, because Baljeet Sir had said on day one that nobody would. Tejas's hand shook a little less.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Sir put on the desk on Wednesday?
qa.a: A tray of matchsticks, tied in bundles of ten.

qa.q: Why did Tejas stare out of the window on Monday?
qa.a: He was panicking and felt scared, so he shut off and stopped listening when the numbers seemed to slide around.

qa.q: Which approach helped Tejas make progress, and why?
qa.a: Hands-on matchstick bundles, patient repetition and a rule that nobody laughs let him see quantities and try without shame.

qa.q: How might Baljeet Sir see the drawings in Tejas's margins?
qa.a: He might see real talent and a way in, which is why he later used drawn birds in groups of ten.

grounding: Tejas panics in maths though good at art, and hands-on materials, patient repetition and no shaming let him progress.
